# Will an old engine have worse fuel efficiency than a new engine?

The short answer is yes, an aging internal combustion engine will almost inevitably exhibit reduced fuel efficiency compared to its factory-fresh state, though the magnitude of that drop depends heavily on maintenance history and driving conditions. Your observation of declining miles per liter after 60,000 kilometers is consistent with standard wear patterns, but it is not solely a function of age. The shift in your commute dynamicsâspecifically transitioning from lower speed limits to higher-speed highwaysâplays a significant role that often gets conflated with engine degradation.

When you drove initially, the lower speed limits dictated a driving profile dominated by acceleration out of stops and cruising at sub-optimal velocities for highway aerodynamics. Modern gasoline engines typically achieve peak thermal efficiency between 60 km/h and 90 km/h on flat roads. If your old commute involved frequent stop-and-go traffic in urban zones with tight speed limits, the engine was spending a disproportionate amount of time operating outside its "sweet spot," burning fuel to overcome friction and inertia rather than maintaining steady-state combustion.

The change to a longer commute with higher speed limits introduces different physical constraints. At highway speeds, aerodynamic drag increases exponentially. The power required to push a car through the air at 100 km/h is significantly higher than at 60 km/h, regardless of how perfect the engine is. However, if your current route involves maintaining a steady cruise on a flatter road compared to the stop-and-go nature of your previous commute, you might actually see improved efficiency despite the "older" engine, provided no mechanical faults have developed.

Mechanical degradation does occur over time and directly impacts fuel economy. You mentioned noticing that the idle sound has become louder and detecting slight piston slap during cold starts. These are auditory indicators of internal clearance increasing due to wear on cylinder walls or piston rings. When these clearances grow, combustion gases leak past the rings into the crankcaseâa phenomenon known as blow-by. This reduces the effective compression ratio during the power stroke and forces the engine control unit (ECU) to enrich the fuel mixture slightly to maintain stable idle speeds, thereby lowering efficiency.

Regarding your oil change observations, there is a technical distinction between viscosity and friction modifiers. You originally used 0W-20, which offers lower internal friction at cold starts but relies heavily on friction-modifier additives to protect worn surfaces. You have since switched to 5W-30. While 5W-30 flows less easily when the engine is cold compared to 0W-20, it generally provides a thicker lubricating film under high heat and load. If your mileage has increased significantly, the engine components may have settled into larger clearances; in this scenario, a slightly higher viscosity oil like 5W-30 can reduce hydraulic friction and prevent metal-to-metal contact better than a thin oil that is breaking down faster. However, if the pistons are wearing excessively, even 5W-30 will eventually be sheared down to the thickness of the base oil, rendering it ineffective.

The durability of special piston coatings is another variable. These coatings, often applied via plasma spraying or similar processes, are designed to reduce thermal expansion and friction. While they significantly extend engine life compared to standard pistons, they are not immune to eventual wear-out. Once the coating wears through to the base material, the engine reverts to standard friction characteristics. If you hear piston slap that persists after the engine warms up, this suggests the coating may be compromised or the underlying cylinder walls are worn beyond the compensation range of the rings.

It is also worth noting the regulatory environment in Finland. High registration and annual taxes based on fuel consumption create a strong economic incentive for manufacturers to tune engines for optimal efficiency under WHTC (World Harmonized Transitory Cycle) conditions, which simulate mixed driving. Manufacturers often calibrate these systems to be slightly "lazy" or rich at wide-open throttle to maximize city-cycle scores, knowing that real-world highway driving will expose the limits of those optimizations. As an engine ages and components wear, it drifts further away from the calibration map designed for a pristine condition.

To diagnose whether your drop in efficiency is purely mechanical or environmental, consider monitoring fuel consumption under controlled conditions. If you can maintain a constant speed of 90 km/h on a flat stretch of road with minimal wind resistance and observe a significant drop in mpg compared to when the car was new, mechanical wear is likely the culprit. If the numbers are stable but the overall distance covered per tank is lower due to route changes, the driving profile has simply shifted. Regular maintenance, including sticking to manufacturer-recommended oil viscosities for your specific mileage bracket and addressing any persistent knocking or slapping noises immediately, remains the most effective way to mitigate these losses.

For developers managing hardware fleets or analyzing IoT telemetry from vehicle sensors, distinguishing between algorithmic efficiency drops and physical degradation is critical. Just as software requires refactoring when performance degrades due to accumulated technical debt, an engine requires interventionâsuch as replacing worn components or adjusting ignition timing maps via ECU flashing (if supported)âto restore original performance metrics.
